#### Propagation — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** Why a stage takes the minimum over its inputs, and what that costs — as three watermark functions over the same stream, treating the two keys as two sources.

`stageWatermark(i)` has the line that matters: `if (w == NONE) { return NONE }`. A source that has produced nothing blocks the claim completely, because silence cannot be distinguished from a pending old event.

`globalWatermark(i)` is the shortcut — max over everything, ignoring sources — and it claims 480 where the safe answer is 200. Step 4 shows the price of being right: window [12:02, 12:04) holds 11, has received every one of its events, and is withheld anyway.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch03-propagation-memory/ch03-propagation-memory.svg" alt="Propagation — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — a source that has said nothing blocks the claim entirely</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch03-propagation-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: a source that has said nothing blocks the claim entirely" width="980">

At `i` = 0 only source "a" has produced anything, so `sourceWatermark("b", 0)` is NONE and this line returns immediately. The stage makes NO claim — not a generous one. Silence is indistinguishable from "an old event is still coming", so it cannot be treated as completeness.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — the claim is the lowest of the inputs, never the highest</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch03-propagation-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: the claim is the lowest of the inputs, never the highest" width="980">

Source "a" has reached 480 and "b" is at 200 — its last event was id 7. `lowest` ends at 200. The stage cannot claim more completeness than its least-complete input, so the quietest source sets the pace.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — a single global watermark would over-claim</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch03-propagation-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: a single global watermark would over-claim" width="980">

`globalWatermark(8)` is 540 − 60 = 480, because it takes the max over ALL events and never asks which source they came from. That is 280s more completeness than source "b" can back — and it is the convenient, wrong answer.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and the correct claim withholds a window that is actually complete</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch03-propagation-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and the correct claim withholds a window that is actually complete" width="980">

Window 120 ([12:02, 12:04)) satisfies both halves: the global watermark would close it and the stage's claim will not. Every event in it has arrived — it holds 11 — and it is withheld because one source went quiet. That is correct, and in production it looks like output silently stopping.

</details>
